22455:
• Every classroom must be equipped with a sensor that continuously measures carbon dioxide in the air, within 6 months.
  • Maximum limit set at 1000 ppm of CO2, lowered to 800 ppm during a declared pandemic period.
  • The department must publish the sensor data on its website every week.
  • An action protocol must be applied by schools when the CO2 standard is exceeded.
  • Every classroom must have an air exchanger or purifier, supplied and paid for by the department, within 12 months.
  • Exchangers and purifiers must be inspected at least every six months, with reports made public.
  • The department must ensure annual follow-up on corrective measures taken as a result of inspections.
22465:
• Requires the government to set by regulation a maximum number of patients per nurse, licensed practical nurse and orderly
  • Applies to emergency departments, surgery, general and specialized medicine, as well as long-term care centres (CHSLDs)
  • Creates a 7-member advisory committee to recommend these ratios to the government
  • The committee includes representatives from unions, professional orders and institution management
  • The committee must submit a report on the impact of the regulation, first in 2023 and then every 5 years
  • This report must be tabled in the National Assembly and studied by a committee
  • The government has one year after the Act is assented to in order to adopt the regulation on ratios
22471:
• Adds to the preamble of the Charter the importance of preserving a healthy environment for human health.
  • Recognizes the right of every person to live in a healthy environment that respects biodiversity.
  • Elevates this right to the status of a fundamental right, like the other rights in the Charter.
  • Removes the restriction limiting this right to the measures and standards provided for by law.
  • This change could facilitate legal recourse based on this environmental right.
22581:
• Amends the Act respecting educational childcare services to guarantee the right to these services.
  • Removes two paragraphs from section 2 of the Act, which limited the scope of this right.
  • The Act would come into force five years after its assent.
22597:
• Makes special educational projects and concentration programs free of charge in public schools, up to $5,000 per year.
  • Includes in the free-of-charge provision selection fees, file-opening fees, test administration fees, and staff training fees.
  • Prohibits school service centres from establishing a special project school in more than one building.
  • Except in special cases: several buildings are permitted only if they are located no more than 250 metres from one another.
22599:
• Amends the Act respecting the Generations Fund, intended to reduce Québec's public debt.
  • Sets a capitalization threshold of $100 billion for this fund.
  • Requires that the allocation and amounts of the Fund remain unchanged until this threshold is reached.
  • Exceptions remain possible only where the Act itself provides for them.
  • The Act would come into force on the date of its official assent.
22639:
• The Minister of Finance will have to ensure gender equality and diversity are considered in budgetary decisions.
  • A report on gender- and diversity-based impacts must be tabled after each budget.
  • This report must also be tabled after an economic update announcing new measures.
  • The competent parliamentary committee must study these tabled reports.
  • The Minister of Finance will publish an annual analysis of the gender- and diversity-based impacts of fiscal measures.
  • The President of the Treasury Board will also publish a similar annual analysis of government spending.

22765:
• Requires the school to provide equivalent educational services if it cannot provide the services required by law.
  • Applies to students with handicaps, social maladjustments or learning disabilities.
  • Requires the authorization of the parent or guardian for a minor student.
  • These services must aim at the full development of the student's personality and social integration.
  • Aims to develop fundamental skills that foster the student's autonomy.
  • The school service centre must ensure that the student can continue on a path toward a secondary school or vocational diploma.
22767:
• Every adult would be presumed to consent to organ and tissue donation after death, unless a refusal was expressed.
  • The person responsible for the removal would have to verify with relatives that no refusal was expressed by the deceased during their lifetime.
  • This verification would not be required in an emergency attested by two physicians to save a life.
  • The registry managed by the Régie would be renamed to include both consents and refusals.
  • The forms would inform people of the presumption of consent and their right to refuse.
  • Minors under 14 years of age would remain subject to mandatory consent from a parent or guardian.
  • The registry maintained by the Chambre des notaires would also be renamed to include refusals.

22797:
• Requires elementary schools, secondary schools and adult education centres to adopt a policy against sexual violence within one year.
  • The policy must include mandatory training, security measures, a complaint process and psychosocial support services.
  • Imposes a code of conduct to govern relationships between staff and students, including students of full age.
  • Sets maximum time limits: 7 days to intervene, 90 days to process a complaint or report.
  • Requires the formation of a committee including management, staff, students and parents to develop and review the policy.
  • Provides for annual accountability reporting on complaints, training and sanctions applied.
  • Allows the minister to impose oversight or have obligations carried out by a third party at the institution's expense in cases of non-compliance.
22799:
• The Caisse de dépôt should ensure that its investments have sustainable social and environmental impacts.
  • Its mission now explicitly includes the sustainable economic development of Québec.
  • The annual report submitted to the Minister of Finance must detail the social and environmental impacts of investments.
  • This report must be tabled in the National Assembly before April 15 each year.
  • The government may set out by regulation the criteria for assessing these impacts.
  • A regulation may also specify how these impacts must be publicly disclosed.
22831:
• The Minister will be required to take temporary residents into account in multi-year immigration planning.
  • The multi-year policy directions will target the number of persons admitted on a temporary or permanent basis.
  • The annual plan will have to specify the expected number of temporary residents, in addition to permanent immigrants.
  • The number of selection decisions provided for in the annual plan will also cover temporary stays.
22899:
• Renders invalid lease clauses that prohibit pets.
  • Applies to leases already in effect, not only to new leases.
  • The government must remove prohibition mentions from mandatory lease forms within 30 days.
  • The definition of "pet" is based on the Animal Welfare and Safety Act.
  • Other existing tenant protections in the Civil Code remain unchanged.
23167:
• Adds an official emblematic insect for Québec, the white admiral (Limenitis arthemis arthemis).
  • Amends the Act respecting the flag and emblems of Québec to include this new symbol.
  • Comes into force upon assent of the Act.
23285:
• Requires authorization from the Minister of the Environment before adding a project to the Québec infrastructure plan.
  • The Minister must refuse a project that jeopardizes the achievement of Québec's greenhouse gas reduction targets.
  • The government will set out by regulation the criteria for analyzing climate impacts, with the assistance of environmental experts.
  • The Minister may impose conditions or restrictions to reduce emissions related to a project.
  • The Minister may amend or add conditions to a project that has already been authorized, if necessary.
  • The Québec infrastructure plan will have to include a report on the emissions and climate impact of projects.
  • Public bodies will be required to provide the Minister with the information necessary for this climate assessment.
23425:
• Prohibits evicting a tenant for the purpose of converting their dwelling into short-term tourist accommodation.
  • Amends section 1959 of the Civil Code of Québec to add this exception.
  • Aims to protect tenants against the conversion of residential dwellings into tourist rentals.
  • The act would come into force on the date of its assent.
23753:
• Requires CEGEPs, universities and other educational institutions to adopt a study-family-work balance policy.
  • Policy intended for student parents or caregivers, to be adopted within 6 months and implemented within 12 months.
  • Creates special statuses: student parent, caregiver, deemed enrolled or enrolled full-time.
  • Provides for leaves, exam accommodations and measures facilitating access to childcare services.
  • Requires a joint committee consulting affected persons to develop and review the policy.
  • Requires institutions to report annually to the minister on the implementation of their policy.
  • Allows the minister to impose oversight measures or have obligations carried out at the institution's expense in cases of non-compliance.
23955:
• Creates a citizen initiative right requiring the BAPE to hold a hearing if a petition reaches certain thresholds.
  • Requires 40,000 signatures (including 5,000 per region, in 3 regions) for a national issue, or 15,000 for a regional issue.
  • The chair and vice-chair of the BAPE will be appointed by the National Assembly, following an in-camera interview with MNAs.
  • Allows the BAPE to require a report on a project's greenhouse gas emissions and its reduction measures.
  • The government will have to publicly justify authorizing a project despite a refusal recommended by the BAPE.
  • Abolishes the Comité consultatif sur les évaluations environnementales stratégiques, whose tasks are transferred to the BAPE.
  • Gives the BAPE the power to recommend that a project be subject to a full environmental assessment.

24137:
• Amends the Act to Foster the Economic and Social Inclusion of Persons and Families to Overcome Poverty for recipients of the Social Solidarity Program.
  • Allows these recipients to earn employment income without a reduction in their benefit.
  • Aligns the amount of permitted employment income with that of the Basic Income Program.
  • The Act would come into force on the date of its official assent.
24211:
• Creates the position of Parliamentary Budget Officer, appointed by the National Assembly for a non-renewable seven-year term.
  • This officer provides non-partisan analysis of Québec's public finances, budget forecasts and economic trends.
  • The officer must produce an annual report on economic outlooks, a portrait of public finances twice a year, and a report on intergenerational equity every three years.
  • Transfers responsibility for certifying the pre-election report on public finances from the Auditor General to this new officer.
  • Members of the National Assembly may request a confidential assessment of the cost of a proposed expenditure or measure.
  • Departments and public bodies must provide the officer with requested documents and information, notwithstanding access to information legislation.
  • The officer and staff benefit from judicial immunities and are bound to secrecy regarding confidential data.

24223:
• Prohibits driving with a blood alcohol level of 50 mg to 80 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood.
  • Immediate licence suspension upon a first offence within this new blood alcohol range.
  • 3-day suspension for a first offence, 7 days for a second offence within 5 years.
  • Suspension of at least 90 days for a third or subsequent offence within 5 years.
  • Licence recovery conditional on an assessment of the person's relationship with alcohol or drugs.
  • Possible requirement to complete an alcohol or drug awareness program.
  • Possibility of requiring the installation of an ignition interlock device in certain cases.
24279:
• Grants each Member the right to visit certain administrative institutions (departments, municipalities, schools, hospitals, etc.).
  • Allows the Member to speak confidentially with any person on site, except ministers.
  • Authorizes the Member to be accompanied by an employee, an expert, and a journalist during the visit.
  • Limits visits to once every three months per institution, for a maximum of two consecutive days.
  • Requires written notice of at least 10 business days before the visit.
  • Allows the institution to refuse or restrict the visit only for serious security reasons.
  • Provides for recourse to the Superior Court if a refusal is deemed unjustified.
24453:
• Aims to reduce food waste by half by 2030 through a national strategy.
  • Requires businesses and manufacturers to offer their unsold goods to organizations before discarding them.
  • Creates a public registry of unsold goods quantities and donation agreements reached.
  • Prohibits deliberately rendering unsold food or goods unfit for consumption.
  • Creates a Repair Fund to encourage the repair of goods and the circular economy.
  • Prevents manufacturers from refusing a warranty if the good was repaired by a third party.
  • Provides for fines of up to $250,000 (individuals) or $1.5 million (businesses).

• Specifies the order of flags: the fleurdelisé on the left, or in the centre if three flags are displayed.

  • Allows the minister to appoint inspectors to verify compliance with the Act.

  • Requires the flag on the building housing the riding office of provincial and federal members.
  • Sets out the rules for disposing of a worn flag (dignified burning or cutting into strips).
  • Requires members to provide a Québec flag free of charge to anyone who requests one.

24617:
• Extends the right to install surveillance mechanisms to users of rehabilitation centres, not just CHSLDs.
  • Targets 4 types of centres: intellectual disability, physical disability, dependency, youth in difficulty.
  • For a user under 14 years of age, the camera must be installed by their representative.
  • Consent to surveillance of a user under 14 years of age must come from their representative.
  • The institutions concerned will have to inform new users of this right upon admission.
  • Adjusts posting and information obligations to include the rehabilitation centres concerned.
  • The Act comes into force upon its official assent.
24727:
• Adds a new section 45.1 to Québec's Charter of human rights and freedoms.
  • Enshrines the right of every person to decent housing.
  • This right includes security of tenure, availability, accessibility and affordability of housing.
  • Draws on international instruments recognizing the right to housing (UN, OAS).
  • The Act comes into force on the date of its assent.
25171:
• Sets the objective of achieving carbon neutrality in Québec by 2050.
  • Requires the government to take the necessary measures to reduce GHG emissions.
  • Imposes a reduction target of at least 37.5% compared to 1990, increasing with each period.
  • Requires a review of the targets every five years.
  • Allows the government to set different targets depending on the sector of activity.
  • Provides for public consultation in a parliamentary committee before setting or revising a target.
  • Requires a public opinion from the advisory committee on climate change before any parliamentary consultation.
25237:
• This bill creates a national digital identity managed by the Minister of Cybersecurity and Digital Technology, to securely access online government services.
  • It also gives the minister more powers over telecommunications, cloud computing and government cybersecurity.
Part 1 Act respecting the Ministère de la Cybersécurité et du Numérique
  • The minister becomes responsible for managing the national digital identity for everyone.
  • The minister provides public bodies with services related to this digital identity.
  • A new registry is created to store and share national digital identity data.
  • The minister becomes the official source of government digital data for digital identity.
  • The minister must propose a comprehensive plan to the government for the state's telecommunications infrastructure.
  • The minister can develop and manage a telecommunications network, without a commercial purpose.
  • Building rental contracts for telecommunications no longer need Treasury Board approval.
  • The minister can offer other specialized technology services, in addition to cloud computing.
Part 2 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale and the Commission des partenaires du marché du travail
  • The Minister of Cybersecurity collaborates on creating a single service window.
Part 3 Act respecting the governance and management of information resources of public bodies and government enterprises
  • Public bodies must use the minister's services for cybersecurity.
  • Public bodies must notify the minister in case of a serious breach of their computer data.
  • The government can extend this notification requirement to other businesses deemed essential.
  • Official data sources must ensure their data is consistent and of good quality.
  • Public bodies must use these official data sources, except for exceptions granted by the government.
  • The chief information officer can now delegate some of their tasks to other people.
Part 4 Act respecting the legal framework for information technology
  • The harmonization committee, which existed before, is removed.
  • It is now the minister, rather than the Treasury Board, who approves businesses offering digital certification services.
  • Tax Administration Act, Health Insurance Act, Land Registry Publicity Regulation, Regulation respecting public bodies' information technology contracts, Regulation respecting government contracts for the rental of buildings: technical adjustments to align with the new rules.

  • No civil action may arise from facts revealed as a result of this Act.
25363:
• Recognizes the right of older persons to remain at home for as long as possible, with appropriate support.
  • Guarantees rights: affordable and adapted housing, protection against abuse, dignified end of life, financial security.
  • Establishes a national strategy for the autonomy and home care of older persons.
  • Requires the government to adopt a five-year action plan with concrete targets for care and housing.
  • Provides for a first action plan to be published within six months of the Act's passage.
  • Assigns the Commission des droits de la personne to ensure respect for these new rights.
  • Provides for tax measures, rent regulation, and financial support for low-income seniors.
25393:
• Makes all women or pregnant persons in Québec eligible for health insurance and prescription drug coverage, regardless of their migratory status.
  • Eliminates the usual waiting period under health insurance for women or pregnant persons.
  • Grants eligibility if the person intends to remain in Québec for more than 6 months, including 2 months after childbirth.
  • Maintains coverage for 2 years after the expected date of childbirth for persons not otherwise eligible.
  • Provides for 12 weeks of eligibility following a pregnancy termination.
  • Requires a medical certificate confirming the pregnancy and expected date of childbirth for registration.
  • Provides that the Act comes into force on the date of its assent, with transitional rules for ongoing cases.

25575:
• Allows municipalities to claim compensation from the government for land transferred to a school service centre.
  • The compensation corresponds to the value of the land as entered on the property assessment roll.
  • Extends from 45 to 60 days the time limit for municipalities to give their opinion on school planning.
  • Requires school service centres to prioritize optimal density of land use.

  • Reduces existing compensation by the amount of any compensation already received for the same land.
25631:
• Creates a common school network bringing together public schools and "contracted" private schools that choose to join it.
  • Prohibits any selection of students upon entry into schools within this common network.
  • Gradually cuts public funding for private schools that refuse to join the common network.
  • Requires free tuition and equal funding for all schools in the network, including special educational projects.
  • Establishes catchment-area school maps, with one designated school per address, reviewed annually.
  • Provides for compensation measures to reduce socio-economic inequalities between school catchment areas.
  • Requires contracted schools to maintain financial transparency, undergo external audits, and be subject to oversight by the minister.

25709:
• The SAAQ will have to send a notice of payment 30 days before the deadline for vehicle registration.
  • A similar notice will also have to be sent 30 days before the driver's licence renewal deadline.
  • These notices must comply with the form and content determined by the SAAQ.
  • An owner or licence holder cannot be found guilty of driving without a valid right if the SAAQ did not send the required notice.
  • The Act comes into force upon its official assent.
25793:
• Strengthens secularism and French in Québec's public and private schools, with new requirements for students and staff.
  • Some rules apply even if they conflict with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms or the Canadian Constitution.
Part 1 Education Act
  • The public school system must respect democratic values, equality between men and women, and the secularism of the state.
  • Students must have their faces uncovered in schools, training centres, and in home schooling.
  • Parents must also have their faces uncovered to receive services from a school service centre.
  • Anyone providing services to students or in contact with them must have their face uncovered.
  • Students must respect equality between men and women and must not engage in bullying related to racism, sexual orientation, or disability.
  • Schools, vocational training centres, and adult education centres must adopt codes of conduct including these requirements.
  • The ban on wearing religious symbols is extended to staff of school service centres and certain contract workers.
  • Staff already in their positions and contracts already underway when the bill was introduced are not subject to this ban.
  • Requests for leave on religious grounds from school staff are more tightly regulated, and may sometimes be refused, including in relation to the school attendance requirement.
  • People who provide services to students and certain board members must act without regard to religious considerations.
  • Staff of school service centres must be guided by the secularism of the state in their decisions and conduct.
  • School service centres must adopt a code of ethics for governing board members.
  • School and centre premises can no longer be used for religious practices.
  • It is forbidden to try to influence, for religious reasons, the exercise of a power or duty provided for by law.
  • Teachers must submit a teaching plan, and principals must evaluate them every year.
  • A new committee on the quality of educational services is created to help school principals.
  • The minister can set the exam schedule and order a school service centre to comply with the law.
  • Certain decisions by the minister, such as suspending a teacher, apply even if the teacher challenges them before the Administrative Tribunal of Québec.
  • French-speaking staff and people working with students must communicate with them, and with each other, only in French.
Part 2 Act on Private Education
  • The same rules on uncovered faces and codes of conduct apply to private educational institutions.
  • Staff of institutions not recognized for subsidies must also have their faces uncovered.
Part 3 Regulation respecting ethics and professional conduct standards
  • Technical adjustments to align with the new rules for school service centres.

26021:
• This bill amends 11 laws and regulations dealing with labour, occupational health and safety, and labour relations in Québec.
  • It changes rules on benefits, fines, unions, arbitration, and the makeup of certain bodies.
Part 1 Act respecting industrial accidents and occupational diseases
  • An officer who works personally for another person can still be recognized as a worker.
  • Changes the rules for calculating the income used to set an injured worker's benefit.
  • The Commission des normes, de l'équité, de la santé et de la sécurité du travail (CNESST) will have to offer negotiation after certain requests for review.
  • Fines are increased if an offence affects the confidentiality of the file of a worker who is a victim of violence, including sexual violence.
Part 2 Labour Code
  • Sets a maximum time limit for choosing an arbitrator and holding the first day of a grievance hearing.
  • Requires the parties to consider mediation before arbitrating a grievance.
  • Sets out when a preparatory meeting must take place before a grievance hearing.
  • Sets rules for sharing evidence before a grievance hearing.
Part 3 Labour Code and Act respecting labour relations in the construction industry
  • Unions must present their audited financial statements to their members every year, or give them a free copy on request.
Part 4 Act respecting labour standards
  • Reduces the length of service needed for a Canadian Forces reservist to take leave for an overseas operation.
  • Expands the reasons a reservist can take leave from work.
  • Allows any employee to take leave if they cannot work because of a public health decision or a disaster.
Part 5 Fines
  • Fines under the Act respecting labour standards are increased, with no specific amounts given in the text.
Part 6 Act respecting occupational health and safety
  • An employer will be able to claim back from the CNESST part of the wages paid to a pregnant or breastfeeding worker reassigned to other duties.
  • Sets rules for recovering an overpayment made to an employer after such a claim.
  • Adds two members to the CNESST board of directors, a union representative and a public employer representative.
  • Allows the CNESST to set construction and safety standards for certain buildings it identifies.
  • Sets out temporary rules on prevention and participation in education and health institutions, until a date set by the government.
  • The minimum time a health and safety representative can spend on their duties will have to vary according to the number of workers at the establishment.
Part 7 Professional Syndicates Act
  • Removes the requirement to be a Canadian citizen to found a professional syndicate or hold a management position in one.
  • Responsibility for this law moves to the Minister of Labour.
Part 8 Act to establish the Administrative Labour Tribunal
  • Only a person authorized by the tribunal will be able to access confidential occupational health and safety files.

  • The vehicle value threshold triggering an additional duty rises from $40,000 to $62,500.
Part 3 Highway Safety Code
  • Electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles lose their exemption from this duty on the portion of value between $40,000 and $75,000.
  • A new additional duty will apply specifically to electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles for their registration or putting into circulation.
Part 4 Act respecting the Institut de la statistique du Québec
  • Clarifies the rules when the Institute collects information for a public body.
  • More researchers linked to a public body will be able to access information held by the Institute for research purposes.

  • Changes the formula for calculating the seizable portion of the income of a person who must pay child or spousal support.
  • Support payments awarded by a court to an adult child will also be excluded from the paying parent's seizable income.

  • A person receiving last-resort financial assistance will no longer have to provide a guarantee when their support payments are collected.

  • The capital of companies related to a company will be taken into account when defining a "large company."
  • Tax information may be shared with the Minister of Finance without the person's consent, to develop economic or budgetary policies.

  • Life insurers will be able to obtain personal information about a deceased person, from Revenu Québec and then the Director of Civil Status, to inform beneficiaries of amounts owed.

  • Municipalities will no longer be allowed to impose a business tax, except for certain fees charged by business development corporations.

26771:
• This bill amends more than a hundred laws and regulations to reorganize government bodies, reduce paperwork and better oversee senior officials.
  • It merges, abolishes or transforms several public bodies and transfers their functions to other existing bodies.
Part 1 Act respecting the National Institute of Excellence in Health and Social Services and Act respecting the Institut national de santé publique du Québec
  • These two bodies merge into one, the Institut québécois de santé et de services sociaux.
Part 2 Act respecting prehospital emergency services
  • Urgences-santé's board of directors will be made up of the same members as Santé Québec's board.
Part 3 Act respecting Héma-Québec
  • This body will take over coordination of organ donations, previously managed by Transplant Québec.
Part 4 Act respecting the Commission d'évaluation de l'enseignement collégial
  • This commission, which evaluated colleges, is being abolished.
Part 5 Act establishing the Office Québec-Monde pour la jeunesse
  • This body is being merged directly into the Ministère des Relations internationales et de la Francophonie.
Part 6 Act respecting the Office franco-québécois pour la jeunesse
  • Its internal operations are being revised.
Part 7 Act respecting the Centre de la francophonie des Amériques
  • This body becomes a business or non-profit organization instead of a public body.
Part 8 Parental Insurance Act
  • The Conseil de gestion de l'assurance parentale is being abolished; Retraite Québec will now manage this plan and its fund.
Part 9 Act respecting the Ministère des Finances
  • The Minister of Finance will have to present an overall financial plan to fight climate change as part of the budget.
Part 10 Act respecting the Ministère du Développement durable, de l'Environnement et des Parcs
  • The government will be able to decide, through a government rule, how to divide surpluses from the Electrification and Climate Change Fund between the Generations Fund and the transportation fund.
Part 11 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Emploi et de la Solidarité sociale
  • This ministry's Information Technology Fund is being abolished, with its assets and debts transferred to the government's general fund.
Part 12 Act respecting the Ministère de l'Enseignement supérieur
  • Fund 3 for university excellence and performance is also being abolished, for the same reason.
Part 13 Act to combat poverty and social exclusion
  • The Fund to Support Autonomous Community Action and the Québec Fund for Social Initiatives are merging into a single fund.
Part 14 Public Service Act
  • The Commission de la fonction publique is being abolished; its tasks move to the Administrative Labour Tribunal.
Part 15 Act respecting administrative justice
  • The Administrative Tribunal of Québec will provide administrative services to the Financial Markets Administrative Tribunal.
Part 16 Act respecting the marketing of agricultural, food and fish products
  • The Régie des marchés agricoles will have fewer vice-chairs and fewer members to decide certain cases.
Part 17 Act respecting the Société de l'assurance automobile du Québec
  • The government will now appoint this corporation's vice-presidents and set their salaries.
Part 18 Act respecting the governance of state-owned enterprises
  • The heads of Hydro-Québec, the Commission de la construction du Québec and other state-owned enterprises will have to appear before a parliamentary committee at least once every four years.
Part 19 Public Administration Act
  • Senior officials (state administrators) will have to act with prudence, efficiency and fairness in their duties.
  • A new state administrator will serve a two-year probationary period before being confirmed in the position.
  • During this probation, the government will be able to dismiss an administrator who was not already a permanent public servant, with a simple 15-day written notice.
Part 20 Act respecting contracting by public bodies
  • Businesses will no longer have to periodically renew their authorization to contract with the government.
Part 21 Act respecting the Centre d'acquisitions gouvernementales
  • Its contracts and those it manages for certain groups of bodies will follow the same rules as government enterprises.
Part 22 Act respecting the Société d'habitation du Québec
  • The government will be able to merge housing bureaus or create new ones for any territory it chooses.
  • The joint management of contributions paid by organizations receiving financial assistance is ending.
Part 23 Act respecting the regulation of the financial sector
  • The Autorité des marchés financiers, which oversees this sector, will have to make certain data and analyses available online.
  • Various coordinating adjustments affect many other laws (health, labour, environment, pensions, French language) to align with these changes, with no major direct effect on the public.
  • Several laws also reduce how often certain reports are required or remove the obligation to produce certain documents, particularly in the financial sector.

Part 6 Act respecting the Québec correctional system

26993:
• This bill simplifies the rules of professional orders (such as doctors, nurses, pharmacists) and gives more powers to certain health professionals.
  • It also changes the rules between pharmacists, manufacturers and pharmacy chains.
Part 1 Professional Code
  • Professional orders will be able to adopt certain regulations without the approval of the Québec Cabinet or the Office des professions, which oversees them.
  • The Office des professions, which oversees professional orders, must approve codes of ethics instead of the Québec Cabinet.
  • The Office des professions now decides which diplomas give access to a professional permit, with the Québec Cabinet's approval.
  • The Office des professions must create a common rule for all orders to settle disagreements over professionals' bills.
  • The Office des professions can create rules that apply to one or more professional orders, after consulting them.
  • The Office des professions alone decides on ethics rules for members of the boards of directors of orders, and can investigate and punish wrongdoing.
  • The public roll of members of a professional order will have to include more information.
  • The minimum number of signatures required to request a special general meeting of an order is changing.
  • People holding a psychotherapist permit obtained elsewhere in Canada under the new rules will be able to practise in Québec.
Part 2 Act respecting nurses
  • Nurses will be able to start examinations and tests in more situations, not only in public health.
  • They will also be able to prescribe examinations, medications, other substances, products and dressings, according to rules to be set later.
  • The rule requiring only section delegates to vote at general meetings is removed.
Part 3 Midwives Act
  • Midwives will be able to prescribe and provide contraceptive methods more often.
  • They will be able to screen more broadly for sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections.
  • They will be able to treat these infections in a person without symptoms whose screening result is positive.
Part 4 Optometry Act
  • Optometrists will be able to prescribe and provide more medications and offer more care, with certain restrictions removed.
Part 5 Dietitians-nutritionists
  • Their scope of practice is updated and they will no longer need a medical prescription to carry out certain reserved activities.
Part 6 Psychotherapy
  • The Interdisciplinary Advisory Council on the Practice of Psychotherapy will cease operating.
  • Marriage and family therapists will be able to practise psychotherapy without a special permit, like psychologists and doctors.
  • The Office des professions will be able to authorize students to carry out certain psychotherapist activities during their training.
Part 7 Act respecting agrologists
  • An act performed by an agrologist counts as practising the profession even if unpaid.
Part 8 Pharmacy Act
  • The Québec Cabinet will be able to allow a pharmacist to prescribe or replace a medication with another made by a company in which they have a financial interest, under specific conditions.
Part 9 Act respecting prescription drug insurance
  • A drug manufacturer will be able to pay certain benefits to an intermediary, such as a pharmacy banner or chain.
Part 10 Regulation respecting the conditions for recognition of a drug manufacturer or wholesaler
  • A manufacturer will also be able to pay these benefits to a drug wholesaler.
  • Several other professional laws (agrologists, land surveyors, the Barreau, notaries, denturology, medical imaging technologists, legal aid, the Charter of the French Language) receive related adjustments linked to these changes.

27053:
• This bill sets rules for exploring and operating underground reservoirs and certain fluids, in addition to existing rules on natural gas and oil.
  • It also allows the government to launch a pilot project in this area.
Part 1 Act respecting the storage of natural gas and respecting natural gas and oil pipelines
  • A person must hold a licence to explore or operate an underground reservoir or certain fluids below ground.
  • The conditions for obtaining a licence will be set by a government rule, without a new vote at the Assembly.
  • The government will be able to set, by regulation, safety standards for work, site closure and site restoration.
  • Certain reservoirs or fluids belonging to the State will be reserved for the State or off-limits to exploration, for example in an urban area or a protected area.
  • The minister will be able to temporarily suspend the granting of a licence on a piece of land while deciding whether to reserve it for the State.
  • A licence holder and a holder of mining rights on the same land will have to agree on their respective activities.
  • The minister will have to monitor sites that were used for carbon storage.
  • Documents sent to the minister by a licence holder will become public, except for exceptions set by regulation.
  • Authorizations to build or use pipelines will now apply only to oil pipelines, not gas pipelines.
  • Conditions for carrying out work will have to be included in municipal regulations.
  • A municipality will be able, in certain cases set by regulation, to block work from being carried out in its territory.
Part 2 Act to end exploration for petroleum and underground reservoirs, the production of petroleum and the exploitation of brine
  • The new bill does not allow the bans already set out in this act to be bypassed.
